t.6.42.1: Seeing the rākṣasa Dhūmrākṣa, of terrible roar, sallying forth, all the vānaras roared aloud, thrilled with joy and eager for battle.
t.6.42.2: Then a tumultuous battle arose between those monkeys and Rākṣasas as they struck one another with terrible trees, spears and maces.
t.6.42.3: On every side the fearsome Vānaras were cut down by the Rākṣasas, and the Rākṣasas too were struck down by the Vānaras with trees and laid level with the ground.
t.6.42.4: The Rākṣasas too, greatly enraged, pierced the Vānaras with sharpened arrows, terrible to behold, straight-flying and fitted with heron feathers.
t.6.42.6: Though being torn apart by the rākṣasas, those mighty vānaras, their fervour roused by indignation, performed their deeds as if unafraid.
t.6.42.5: They, with terrible maces, with sharp-edged spears and spiked hammers, with dreadful, gleaming iron bars, and with keenly sharpened tridents as well,
t.6.42.7: Those leaders of the monkey troops, their limbs pierced by arrows and their bodies pierced by spears, seized trees and rocks there.
t.6.42.8: Those monkeys of fearsome speed, roaring here and there, crushed the dreadful rākṣasas and called out their own names.
t.6.42.9: Then there arose a wondrous and terrible battle between the monkeys and the rākṣasas, fought with rocks of many kinds and with many-branched trees.
t.6.42.10: Some rākṣasas were crushed by the vānaras, who bore the look of victors; and some, those drinkers of blood, rained blood from their mouths.
t.6.42.11: Some were torn open at their flanks, some were heaped into piles by trees; some were crushed to powder by rocks, and some were ripped apart by teeth.
t.6.42.13: The rākṣasas were slashed across their faces with sharp nails by the swift vānaras of fearsome valor, who leapt upon them again and again.
t.6.42.12: With banners crushed and broken, with donkeys struck down, with chariots shattered, and with the night-rangers fallen on the ground
t.6.42.14: Their faces pale, their hair dishevelled, stupefied by the smell of blood, they fell once more upon the surface of the earth.
t.6.42.15: But other rākṣasas of terrible prowess, exceedingly enraged, rush upon the monkeys with their bare palms alone, whose touch was like that of a thunderbolt.
t.6.42.16: As they rushed forward in their swift onset, they were struck down by the still swifter monkeys with fists, feet, teeth and trees.
t.6.42.17: But seeing his army put to flight, Dhūmrākṣa, the bull among rākṣasas, in his fury wrought slaughter among the vānaras who were eager for battle.
t.6.42.18: Some of the monkeys, crushed by spears, streamed with blood; others, struck by maces, fell upon the surface of the earth.
t.6.42.20: Some of the forest-dwellers, struck down by the enraged rākṣasas in battle, lay on the ground drenched in blood; others, put to flight, vanished.
t.6.42.19: Some were crushed by iron clubs, some were torn apart by javelins; others, struck down by sharp-edged spears, writhed in agony and breathed their last.
t.6.42.21: Some, their hearts split open, were laid low on one side; some were torn apart by tridents, and some streamed forth with their entrails.
t.6.42.22: That great and most terrible battle, crowded with monkeys and rākṣasas, abounding in weapons and filled with rocks and trees, shone forth.
t.6.42.23: The music of battle shone forth, sweet with bowstrings for its lute-strings, accompanied by the rhythm of gasping death-rattles, with deep rumbling roars for its song.
t.6.42.24: But Dhūmrākṣa, bow in hand, laughing at the forefront of the battle, scattered those monkeys in all directions with showers of arrows.
t.6.42.25: Seeing the army harassed by Dhūmrākṣa and distressed, Māruti, greatly enraged, seized a huge rock and charged forward.
t.6.42.26: His eyes doubly copper-red with rage, he whose valor equalled his father's hurled that rock toward the chariot of Dhūmrākṣa.
t.6.42.28: That rock, having crushed his chariot together with its wheels and pole, with its horses, with its banner and with his bow, fell to the ground.
t.6.42.27: Seeing the rock hurtling toward him, he raised his mace in alarm, leapt swiftly from his chariot, and stood upon the ground.
t.6.42.29: Having shattered his chariot, Hanumān, the son of Māruta, wrought a slaughter of the rākṣasas with trees, complete with their trunks and branches.
t.6.42.30: Rākṣasas, their heads split open and drenched in blood, and others crushed by trees, fell upon the surface of the earth.
t.6.42.31: Having put the rākṣasa army to flight, Hanūmān, the son of the Wind-god, seized a mountain peak and rushed upon Dhūmrākṣa.
t.6.42.32: As Hanūmān came rushing toward him, the valiant Dhūmrākṣa raised his mace and, roaring loudly, suddenly charged at him.
t.6.42.33: Then Dhūmrākṣa, enraged, swiftly brought down that mace, studded with many spikes, upon the head of Hanumān.
t.6.42.34: Struck there by that fearsome-looking mace, the monkey, who had the strength of the Wind, paid no heed to the blow and brought a mountain peak crashing down upon the middle of Dhūmrākṣa's head.
t.6.42.35: Struck by a mountain peak, he, his whole body shaken and trembling, suddenly fell to the ground like a mountain shattered to pieces.
t.6.42.36: Seeing Dhūmrākṣa slain, the night-roaming rākṣasas who remained of those killed, terrified and being struck down by the monkeys, entered Laṅkā.
t.6.42.37: But the great-souled son of Pavana, having slain his foe and spread rivers flowing with blood all around, though wearied from killing the enemy, was filled with joy as he was honored by the monkeys.
